item.title: I’m Done Romanticizing and Optimizing My Life
item.dc:creator: Margaret Cole
item.description: Why I’m done treating a balanced life like a trend, and the one question to ask before you try the next one.
item.content:encoded:
As we all know, social media is an echo chamber, and mine has been shouting from the rooftops for months:

“A Day in My Life Romanticizing the Little Things”

“10 Ways to Optimize Your Morning Routine”

“Ways to Romanticize Your Life This Fall”

“Looksmaxxing as a Corporate Girl”

“Glow Up in 3 Months”

And on and on and on. And these aren’t just Instagram trends. I tried to escape the noise by going to Substack instead, because surely the content there would feel more enriching. Somehow, it was almost worse. Almost every single article I came across was a step-by-step guide promising to fix your life in 90 days.

And don’t get me wrong: since I started writing for The VIRI Edit, I have absolutely fallen into the trap of giving quick life advice. But this morning, when I sat down to figure out what my next article would be, I scrolled through Instagram and Substack looking for inspiration and almost immediately logged off in frustration.

I’m officially done romanticizing and optimizing my life. Okay, now you might be thinking to yourself, but aren’t these practices inherently good for you? To which I would reply: to an extent, yes, they are.

I’m getting ahead of myself. Let’s first establish what these terms even mean. Romanticizing your life is choosing to treat ordinary moments with attention and appreciation. In practice, this often means making small rituals feel intentional. On social media, this can take the form of:

  • Lighting a candle while you make dinner
  • Journaling and meditating first thing in the morning
  • Slicing lemons to put in your water
  • Doing a slow, multi-step skincare routine

The whole idea is that you’re giving added attention to the little things that can make your life feel more pleasant. Sounds nice, right?

All right, now a quick rundown of optimization. Optimizing your life has become a trend that focuses on deliberately improving how you use your time, energy and resources to get more of what you value with less waste. Where romanticizing is about how you experience your days, optimizing is about how you structure them. In practice, optimizing may look like:

  • Creating systems and routines
  • Tracking and measuring things like your sleep, your budget and how you spend your time
  • Cutting friction by saying no to commitments that drain you or by habit stacking

On their own, romanticizing and optimizing parts of your day can add great value to your life. However, it’s the superficial, performative side of these trends that has frustrated me to no end. Why should living a balanced, fulfilling life have to feel like a trend to hop on? Instead of romanticizing your November, why can’t you just find routines that work for you and stay consistent with them?

Trends often lead us to take action for the wrong reasons. Most of the time, this is fairly harmless. Say polka dots start trending, and all of a sudden you subconsciously decide, “Hey, I think polka dots are cute,” so the next time you walk by Urban Outfitters, you buy that $25 polka dot top (definitely not based on a true story). Spending a few extra dollars here and there on an internet trend isn’t the end of the world, but to me, there’s a big difference between that kind of trend and the trend of romanticizing and optimizing your lifestyle.

These trends get at a much deeper issue: your fundamental values and priorities. If you’re really going to transform your lifestyle, perhaps by waking up early, exercising, reading and meditating, it should be because each of these practices ties to a greater goal or reason for being, not because @wellnessgirly123’s routine looks so aesthetic.

Your goals and values are sacred. They deserve far more time and reflection than a trend could ever give them. With trends, we often operate on autopilot, but our goals and routines should be intentional.

All of this is to say: yes, there are undoubtedly parts of my life that I romanticize and have worked to optimize, but that’s because they help me reach a bigger dream or goal. So yes, I do wake up at 5 a.m. and exercise. Yes, I do sit down to do deep work and read after lighting a candle and putting on eye patches. And yes, I do have systems and tracking for all of it. But each of these practices has taken months, if not years, to develop, and they all serve a greater purpose than following a trend.

So the next time you start reading a self-help article with 10 ways to romanticize your life this fall, really ask yourself: Do these practices align with my larger goals and values? If the answer is yes, light the candle. If it’s no, you have my full permission to log off and just live your life, no trend required.
